problem.title: Double-Checked Locking & Memory Barriers
problem.prompt: After migrating a high-throughput Java 21 microservice from x86-64 (TSO) to AWS Graviton ARM64 instances, the service experiences rare `NullPointerException`s and zeroed configuration fields during startup bursts. The culprit is a lazy-initialized `RoutingTable` singleton using Double-Checked Locking (DCL) without `volatile`. Explain the exact hardware/JIT reordering failure, fix the DCL implementation with minimal read-path overhead, and compare it against alternative safe lazy-initialization patterns.
requirements: Explain why non-volatile DCL fails intermittently on ARM64 while appearing to work on x86-64.
Provide a memory-model-safe DCL implementation in Java that minimizes volatile read overhead on the hot path.
Contrast `volatile` memory barriers against `VarHandle` acquire/release fences and the Initialization-on-Demand Holder idiom.
Handle constructor exceptions safely without poisoning the singleton.
constraints: Read path is called > 500,000 times/sec per pod; cannot acquire a `synchronized` lock on every read.
Target architecture is ARM64 (weak memory model) running Java 21.
Initialization involves loading a 20 MB routing snapshot, so eager startup initialization is discouraged if unused.

stages.learnerPrompt: Explain the exact 3-step instruction sequence during `instance = new RoutingTable()` and why ARM64 exposes a bug that x86-64 hides.

referenceMaterial.summary: x86-64 TSO preserves store-store order in hardware, whereas ARM64 allows the pointer store to become visible before constructor field stores.
approachSteps: Break `new RoutingTable()` into: (1) allocate, (2) init fields, (3) assign `instance`.
Show how (1) -> (3) -> (2) passes `if (instance != null)` on Thread B while fields are still `null`/`0`.
tradeOffs: Understanding hardware memory models prevents subtle cross-architecture production outages.
alternatives: Testing under JCStress on ARM64 to surface weak-memory-model races in CI.
failureModes: Assuming `final` fields alone save DCL if the `instance` reference itself is read without a barrier (in practice `final` has freeze semantics, but non-final fields or JIT optimizations still break).

stages.learnerPrompt: Write the corrected Double-Checked Locking implementation in Java, optimizing the fast read path.
Review the production-grade Java DCL implementation using `volatile` and a local variable cache.

referenceMaterial.summary: Use `volatile` for happens-before safety and a local variable `result` to perform only one volatile read on the hot path.
approachSteps: Read `RoutingTable result = instance;` once before the outer `if`.
tradeOffs: Local variable caching avoids a second `ldar` instruction on every fast-path call.
failureModes: Assigning `instance = new RoutingTable(...)` inside `synchronized` without `volatile` still fails.

stages.learnerPrompt: When should you use the Initialization-on-Demand Holder idiom instead of DCL, and when does the Holder idiom break down?

referenceMaterial.summary: Use the Holder idiom for parameterless singletons with zero-barrier reads; avoid it when initialization needs runtime arguments or must be retryable on failure.
approachSteps: JVM class initialization lock guarantees thread-safe lazy loading of `Holder.INSTANCE`.
If `new RoutingTable()` throws in `<clinit>`, the class is permanently poisoned with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
tradeOffs: Holder has ~0.5ns read cost vs. ~1.5ns for volatile DCL, but lacks retryability and runtime parameters.
alternatives: Java `enum` singleton (eagerly initialized on first enum reference).
failureModes: Using Holder for I/O-dependent initialization that can fail transiently during boot.

stages.learnerPrompt: What happens if `RoutingTable` must also be hot-reloaded every 5 minutes without locking readers?

referenceMaterial.summary: Swap an immutable `RoutingTable` instance atomically via `AtomicReference` or a `volatile` field updated by a background scheduler.
approachSteps: Build the new immutable `Map.copyOf(...)` off the request thread.
Atomically publish the new reference via `volatile` write (`instance = nextTable`).
Readers continue using `RoutingTable r = instance;` with zero locks.
tradeOffs: Copy-on-write immutable swap gives lock-free reads at the cost of holding 2x table memory briefly during swap.
alternatives: `StampedLock` optimistic reads for fine-grained mutable structures.
failureModes: Mutating the underlying `Map` in place instead of swapping an immutable snapshot.

stages.learnerPrompt: How would you prove in CI that your singleton implementation is free of weak-memory-model races?

referenceMaterial.summary: Use OpenJDK JCStress on ARM64 runners to exhaustively test interleavings of `Actor` initialization and `Observer` reads.
approachSteps: Annotate a test class with `@JCStressTest` and `@Outcome(id = "0", expect = FORBIDDEN)`.
Run on Graviton/ARM64 CI runners where weak memory ordering actively manifests.
tradeOffs: JCStress catches JMM bugs in seconds that otherwise appear once a month in production.
failureModes: Running concurrency stress tests only on x86-64 laptops.

spark.summary: Fix an intermittent ARM64 production crash where a non-volatile Double-Checked Locking singleton exposes a partially constructed object to concurrent threads.
spark.keyTakeaway: Without `volatile`, the JVM and ARM64 CPU can reorder pointer assignment before constructor completion; fix it with `volatile` (plus a local variable cache) or the lock-free Initialization-on-Demand Holder idiom.

problem.prompt: After migrating a high-throughput Java 21 microservice from x86-64 (TSO) to AWS Graviton ARM64 instances, the service experiences rare `NullPointerException`s and zeroed configuration fields during startup bursts. Explain the exact hardware/JIT reordering failure, fix the DCL implementation with minimal read-path overhead, and compare it against alternative safe lazy-initialization patterns.
requirements: Explain why non-volatile DCL fails intermittently on ARM64 while appearing to work on x86-64.
Provide a memory-model-safe DCL implementation in Java that minimizes volatile read overhead on the hot path.
Contrast `volatile` memory barriers against `VarHandle` acquire/release fences and the Initialization-on-Demand Holder idiom.
Handle constructor exceptions safely without poisoning the singleton.
constraints: Read path is called > 500,000 times/sec per pod; cannot acquire a `synchronized` lock on every read.

concept.whyItMatters: x86-64's Total Store Order (TSO) masks StoreStore reordering bugs in development, but migrating to ARM64/Graviton exposes partially constructed objects under load—causing silent data corruption or NPEs.
whenToUse: Lazy initialization of expensive, thread-shared resources (connection pools, ML models, routing tables) where read latency matters.
When runtime arguments are required during lazy construction (where static class-holder cannot pass parameters).
whenNotToUse: Parameterless singletons, where the Initialization-on-Demand Holder idiom or an `enum` singleton is simpler and faster.
Fast-to-construct objects that can simply be `final` fields initialized eagerly.
keyPoints: Object construction has three steps: (1) allocate memory, (2) run constructor, (3) assign reference to `instance`. Without `volatile`, JIT/CPU can execute (1) -> (3) -> (2).
Thread B seeing `instance != null` skips the `synchronized` block and reads uninitialized fields (`0` / `null`) because no `happens-before` edge exists.
Adding `volatile` inserts a `StoreStore`/`LoadLoad` barrier (e.g., `stlr`/`ldar` on ARM64), guaranteeing the constructor completes before the reference becomes visible.
Caching `RoutingTable local = instance;` in a local variable reduces `volatile` reads on the fast path from two to one.
terms: Happens-Before Relationship: A Java Memory Model guarantee that memory writes by one statement are visible to another subsequent statement.
StoreStore / LoadLoad Barrier: CPU fence instructions (`dmb ish` / `stlr` on ARM64) that prevent stores or loads from being reordered across the barrier.
Partially Constructed Object: An allocated heap object whose reference is published to other threads before its constructor finishes initializing its fields.

tradeOffs.pro: DCL supports runtime parameters and retryable exception handling during initialization.
tradeOffs.con: Requires a `volatile` load (`ldar` on ARM64) on every read, unlike a static `final` holder field.

tradeOffs.factor: Local Variable Cache (`T r = instance;`) vs. Direct Field Reads
tradeOffs.pro: Cuts volatile loads in half on the uncontended fast path (up to 25% faster in tight loops).

failureModes.name: Missing `volatile` Keyword
failureModes.description: Thread B observes a non-null `instance` reference before Thread A writes the constructor's fields to shared cache.
failureModes.mitigation: Declare `private static volatile RoutingTable instance;` (or use `VarHandle.setRelease`/`getAcquire`).

failureModes.name: Class-Holder Poisoning on Exception
failureModes.description: If a static holder's `<clinit>` throws an exception once, the JVM marks the class `erroneous` (`NoClassDefFoundError`) forever.
failureModes.mitigation: Use DCL with `try/catch` when initialization depends on flaky external I/O so subsequent calls can retry.

failureModes.name: Non-Final Fields Without Safe Publication
failureModes.description: Publishing a mutable object without `volatile` or `final` fields lets readers see stale default values.
failureModes.mitigation: Make all fields inside the singleton `final` and publish via `volatile`.

commonMistakes: Believing `synchronized` inside the inner `if` protects the outer `if (instance == null)` check.
Reading `instance` twice on the fast path (`if (instance == null) ... return instance;`) instead of caching in a local variable.
Assuming x86-64 test passes prove thread safety on ARM64.
Using `DCL` when a simple `private static class Holder { static final T INSTANCE = new T(); }` would work with zero barriers.

sections.content:
## The Problem

In Java, `instance = new RoutingTable()` is not atomic. It compiles to: (1) allocate heap memory, (2) initialize fields in the constructor, (3) store the pointer into `instance`. Without `volatile`, the JIT compiler and ARM64's weak memory model may reorder (3) before (2). Thread B reads `instance != null`, bypasses `synchronized`, and dereferences uninitialized fields.

## Requirements & Constraints

- **Throughput**: > 500,000 reads/sec per pod; lock-free fast path.
- **Architecture**: ARM64 (Graviton) weak memory model under Java 21.
- **Resilience**: Must allow retry if loading the 20 MB routing snapshot fails transiently.

## Performance & Barrier Overhead

- **`synchronized` on every read**: ~25-40ns uncontended, collapses under contention.
- **Volatile DCL (2 reads)**: ~2-3ns on ARM64 (`ldar`).
- **Volatile DCL (1 read via local var)**: ~1.2-1.8ns.
- **Holder Idiom**: ~0.5ns (plain `ldr` after class initialization), but cannot retry if `<clinit>` throws.

edges.label: construct fields
edges.title: Initialize Object Fields
edges.description: Thread A acquires monitor lock and populates all RoutingTable fields in its store buffer.

edges.label: stlr (StoreStore)
edges.title: Volatile Release Store
edges.description: Writing `volatile instance` emits `stlr` on ARM64, flushing all constructor writes before publishing the pointer.

edges.label: ldar (LoadAcquire)
edges.title: Single Volatile Read
edges.description: Thread B reads `RoutingTable r = instance;` once using `ldar`, establishing a happens-before edge.

edges.label: r != null
edges.title: Lock-Free Return
edges.description: Seeing `r != null`, Thread B returns `r` directly without entering `synchronized` or re-reading `instance`.

edges.label: retry on throw
edges.title: Safe Exception Recovery
edges.description: If snapshot loading throws inside `synchronized`, `instance` stays `null` so the next caller can retry.

data.caption: Volatile release/acquire barriers pair with a local variable cache for safe, lock-free reads on ARM64.

sections.content:
## Detailed Design

### 1. Safe & Optimized Volatile DCL
Use `private static volatile RoutingTable instance;` and cache it in a local variable (`RoutingTable result = instance;`). If `result == null`, enter `synchronized (RoutingTable.class)`, re-check `result = instance;`, and construct if still `null`.

### 2. Why x86-64 Hid the Bug
x86-64 guarantees Total Store Order (TSO): stores cannot be reordered after other stores. ARM64 allows independent stores (constructor field writes vs. `instance` pointer store) to become visible out of order unless `dmb`/`stlr` barriers are emitted.

## Failure Handling

- **Transient Snapshot Load Failure**: Because construction happens inside `synchronized` before assigning `instance`, an exception leaves `instance == null`, allowing the next request to retry cleanly (unlike static Holder classes which permanently fail with `NoClassDefFoundError`).

## Final Answer

Declare `instance` as **`volatile`** to emit ARM64 `stlr`/`ldar` memory barriers that prevent constructor-pointer reordering, cache `instance` in a **local variable** to halve volatile reads on the 500K/s hot path, and reserve the **Initialization-on-Demand Holder** for parameterless, non-retryable singletons.
